claims.text: The equimolar high-entropy diboride (Hf0.2Zr0.2Ta0.2Nb0.2Ti0.2)B2 can be synthesized by mechanical alloying followed by spark plasma sintering.
Replacing TiB2 with this high-entropy boride will improve resistance to molten-aluminum corrosion.
Conventional TiB2 components undergo notable degradation in molten aluminum.
The proposed intervention is to replace a binary boride with a mechanically alloyed and spark-plasma-sintered high-entropy boride.
Hot-dip aluminum-plating components operate in molten aluminum at around 1500 °C under oxidative conditions.
The intervention produces a single-phase, chemically homogeneous high-entropy boride microstructure.
The high-entropy boride forms stable, protective oxide layers such as HfO2 and ZrO2.
Increased mixing entropy and microstructural refinement from mechanical alloying produce a uniform distribution of refractory metals.
Oxidation of the equimolar high-entropy diboride produces non-volatile oxides in the relevant temperature range.
The oxides formed by the high-entropy boride are high-melting.
The oxide scale reduces interaction with and dissolution by molten aluminum.
The high-entropy boride will have lower mass loss than TiB2 during molten-aluminum exposure.
The high-entropy boride will retain structural integrity better than TiB2 during molten-aluminum exposure.
The high-entropy boride has superior oxidation resistance to identically processed TiB2.
Significant oxidation and degradation of conventional TiB2 are documented under the proposed molten-aluminum baseline conditions.
The improvement should remain effective near 1500 °C under hot-dip aluminum-plating conditions.
Unexpected phase transformations or low-melting oxide formation could limit effectiveness.
The magnitude of improvement and long-term stability under cyclic thermal stress are not yet quantified.

A controlled comparison will expose TiB2 and the high-entropy boride to identical molten-aluminum conditions at 1500 °C and measure mass change, microstructure, phases, and retained mechanical properties.
Failure to obtain a statistically significant mass-loss reduction, improved structural integrity, or a more protective oxide scale relative to TiB2 will falsify the hypothesis.
